title: Problem 3.1
statement_text: Determine whether or not there exists a function $r_{0}\colon\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R}$ such that the following holds. For each $n\geq 1$, let $\chi_{1},\ldots,\chi_{m}\colon\binom{[n]}{2}\to\mathcal{C}_{r}$ be independent uniformly random $r$-edge-colorings. If $r=r(n)$ satisfies $r(n)<r_{0}(n)$, then with high probability, there does not exist a rainbow stacking of $\chi_{1},\ldots,\chi_{m}$. If $r=r(n)$ satisfies $r(n)>r_{0}(n)$, then with high probability, there exists a rainbow stacking of $\chi_{1},\ldots,\chi_{m}$.
context_text: Let $\mathfrak{S}_n$ be the symmetric group on $[n]$, $K_n$ the complete graph on $[n]$, and $\mathcal{C}_r$ a set of $r$ colours. A rainbow stacking of edge-colourings $\chi_1,\dots,\chi_m:\binom{[n]}{2}\to\mathcal{C}_r$ is a tuple $(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_m)\in\mathfrak{S}_n^m$ such that for each edge $e$ the colours $\chi_1(\sigma_1^{-1}(e)),\dots,\chi_m(\sigma_m^{-1}(e))$ are all distinct; informally, the $m$ coloured copies of $K_n$ are stacked on top of each other so that no edge lies above another edge of the same colour. Here $m\ge2$ is fixed, the colourings are independent and uniformly random, and 'with high probability' means with probability tending to $1$ as $n\to\infty$. The authors prove that for any $\omega(n)\to\infty$, there is w.h.p. no rainbow stacking if $r\le\frac{m\binom{n}{2}}{2\log(n!)}-\frac{\omega(n)}{(\log n)^2}$, and w.h.p. there is one if $r\ge\frac{m\binom{n}{2}}{2\log(n!)}+\frac{2m-1}{3}+\frac{m}{2\log n}+\frac{\omega(n)}{(\log n)^2}$. So the transition occurs within an interval of length roughly $(2m-1)/3$ around a critical value of order $n/\log n$, and the problem asks whether it is even sharper, i.e. governed by a single threshold function $r_0$. The authors compare with the $2$-point concentration of the independence number of $G(n,1/2)$, which is less dramatic since that quantity is only $O(\log n)$.

title: Question 3.3
statement_text: Is it true that when $n$ is odd, every pair of proper edge-colorings of $K_{n}$ admits a rainbow stacking?
context_text: Let $\mathfrak{S}_n$ be the symmetric group on $[n]$, $K_n$ the complete graph on $[n]$, and $\mathcal{C}_r$ a set of $r$ colours. A rainbow stacking of edge-colourings $\chi_1,\dots,\chi_m:\binom{[n]}{2}\to\mathcal{C}_r$ is a tuple $(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_m)\in\mathfrak{S}_n^m$ such that for each edge $e$ the colours $\chi_1(\sigma_1^{-1}(e)),\dots,\chi_m(\sigma_m^{-1}(e))$ are all distinct; informally, the $m$ coloured copies of $K_n$ are stacked on top of each other so that no edge lies above another edge of the same colour. The question concerns $m=2$ proper edge-colourings (no two edges sharing a vertex get the same colour), with any number of colours. The authors show that not every pair of proper edge-colourings has a rainbow stacking: if $n=2^k-2$ with $k\ge2$, removing two pairs $\{u_1,v_1\}$, $\{u_2,v_2\}$ with $u_1+v_1=u_2+v_2$ from $\mathbb{F}_2^k$ and colouring each edge $\{x,y\}$ by $x+y$ gives two proper colourings of $K_n$ with no rainbow stacking (a construction from transversals in Latin squares). This Cayley sum-graph construction does not work for large $n\ne2^k-2$, by a result of Müyesser and Pokrovskiy. Motivated by this and by Ryser's conjecture on transversals in Latin squares of odd order, the authors ask about odd $n$. The answer is yes for $n=3$ (by inspection) and $n=5$ (by computer search); a general resolution seems difficult, and it may be easier to start with proper colourings in which no colour appears many times.
